div.head: II As 2
div.ab: Ond we cwædon be þam hlafordleasan mannum, ðe mon nán ryht ætbegytan ne mæg, þæt mon beode ðære mægþe, ðæt hi hine to folcryhte gehamette ⁊ him hlaford finden on folcgemote.
Be lafordleasum mannum. And we cwædon be ðam hlafordleasum mannum, ðe nan man nan riht ætbegytan ne mæg, þæt man bude ðære mægðe, þæt hi hine to rihte gehamette ⁊ him hlaford fundon on folcgemote.
⁊ we cwædon be ðam hlafordleasum mannum, þe mon nan riht ætbegitan ne mæg, þæt mon bude þær mæg, þæt heo hine to ryht gehamette ⁊ him hlaford finde ⁊ folcgemote.
Et diximus de illis qui dominos non habent, de quibus rectum difficile conquiritur aut nullum, ut precipiatur cognationi eorum, ut eos ad rectum adducat et dominum eis inueniant in conuentu publico.
[Be lafordleasum mannum.] Ond we cwædon be þam hlafordleasan mannum, ðe mon nán ryht ætbegytan ne mæg, þæt mon beode ðære mægþe, ðæt hi hine to folcryhte gehamette ⁊ him hlaford finden on folcgemote.

(Von herrenlosen Leuten. B) Und wir bestimmten über solche herrenlosen Leute, von denen sich keine Rechtserfüllung erlangen lässt, dass man der Sippe [derselben] gebiete, dass sie einen solchen fürs (ordentliche H) Gericht sesshaft mache, und [sie] sollen ihm in der Volksversammlung einen Herrn ausfindig machen.

(Of lordless men. B) And we determined concerning those lordless men from whom no legal satisfaction can be obtained, that the kindred [of the same] be commanded to settle such a one at home for the (regular, H) court, and [they] are to find him a lord at the public assembly.

With regard to lordless men from whom no [legal] satisfaction can be obtained, we have declared that their relatives shall be commanded to settle them in a fixed residence where they will become amenable to public law, and find them a lord at a public meeting.

Concerning lordless men. And we pronounced about those lordless men, from whom no justice can be obtained, that one should order their kindred to fetch back such a person to justice and to find him a lord in public meeting.
div.note: So reads ‘⁊ folcgemote’; Liebermann would correct to ‘on’.

Vgl. Gl Gefolge 9 b-e. Andere German. Polizeivorschriften über Beheimatung der nicht mit Land Angesessenen vergleicht Maurer in Kr. Übsch. I 427. Der Staat ruft die Vassallität zu Hilfe, um die mangels Grundbesitzes und fester Wohnung unpfändbaren Verklagten vor Gericht zu zwingen (Maitland Domesday 284). Nicht alle ohne echtes Grundeigen fielen unter diese Klasse; Dörfler und Bürger auf geliehenem Boden, also zu Fron oder Zins pflichtig, brauchten, weil sesshaft, nicht immer einem Herrn kommendiert zu sein

Cf. Gl Gefolge 9 b-e. Maurer in Kr. Übsch. I 427 compares other Germanic police regulations on providing a domicile for those not settled on land. The state calls vassalage to its aid in order to compel to appear in court defendants who, lacking landed property and a fixed dwelling, cannot be distrained upon (Maitland Domesday 284). Not all those without true allodial land fell into this class; villagers and burgesses on leased land, and thus liable to labour service or rent, did not always need to be commended to a lord, since they were settled

riht entspricht dem Archetyp, laut des Stammbaums der Hss., nicht H's folcriht; voreilig haftete dieses Schreibers Auge auf folc in nächster Z. ‘Nach Volksrecht’ Schmid: möglich, aber farblos; vgl. vielmehr Wb S. 185 Sp. 2 Z. 1

riht corresponds to the archetype, according to the stemma of the MSS, not H's folcriht; this scribe's eye prematurely fixed on folc in the next line. ‘According to folk-law’ Schmid: possible, but colourless; cf. rather Wb p. 185 col. 2 l. 1

Entweder ist Ellipse des Pronomens anzunehmen — was sonst in Gesetzen nach Af kaum mehr vorkommt — oder mægð ist im ersten Satzteil mit Sing., im zweiten mit Plural verbunden. — S. Gl Sippe 16 b

Either an ellipsis of the pronoun must be assumed — which hardly occurs any longer in the laws after Af — or mægð is construed with a singular in the first clause and with a plural in the second. — See Gl Sippe 16 b

note.label: back
note.seg: gehamettan has been assumed from this context and from its etymology to mean “to domicile”, but one should compare the O.E. version of the Capitula of Theodulf (ed. A.S.Napier (1916), pp. 115f.), where the words omnes debitores uestros repetitis (Douai version: “you exact of all your debtors”) of Isaiah lviii. 3, are rendered ealle eowre gyltendras ge hametað. A rendering “bring back”, or “bring home” would suit very well the only other recorded instance, i.e. Birch, No. 599; he moste þa inberðan menn hamettan to Eblesburnan, “he might bring home to Ebblesbourne the persons born on the estate”.
